subtype: Approach: pricing by costs and time [Thinking]
passage: “Shalini, you asked how I picked my bookmark price, so here's the honest version. At first I charged ten rupees because everyone smiled and said ‘so cheap!’ Then one night I counted. Card, thread and glue came to about six rupees each, and every bookmark took twenty minutes. Ten minus six is four rupees for twenty minutes. That's twelve rupees an hour, if I'm lucky. I looked at what the stationery shop and the lady next door charged for similar ones, twenty-five to thirty-five. So I set thirty. Two people grumbled. My stomach did a little flip. But I could keep making them, and I finally understood that pricing low to please everyone meant I'd quit by Diwali. I'm Alka, by the way.”

qa.q: How many minutes did each bookmark take?
What did Alka feel on realising the ten-rupee price left so little?
qa.a: Worry mixed with sober clarity: Alka saw that pleasing buyers with a tiny price would end in giving up.

qa.q: What could Alka try if two buyers still grumble, and why?
qa.a: Alka could offer a set of bookmarks at a bundle price or a simpler design at a lower price, since that keeps costs and time covered while giving buyers a choice.

qa.q: How might a buyer used to the ten-rupee price see the change?
qa.a: A buyer may be surprised at first, but seeing the price match neighbours' similar work and the effort involved could make it feel fair.

grounding: A student adds material costs and time, compares with neighbours, and sets a fair price after seeing that underpricing is unsustainable.

subtype: Approach: pricing by costs and time [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Hemant, and my neighbour Gargi started selling handmade clay earrings from her balcony this year. At first she charged forty rupees a pair, because, she said, "Nobody will pay more."

She was always tired. I'd see her working at midnight, and she ran out of clay every week.

One evening she sat on the steps with a notebook and a calculator, muttering aloud. "Clay, paint, hooks: twenty-two rupees. One hour per pair. The girl in the next lane charges a hundred and twenty for the same thing." She stared at the page. "So I'm getting eighteen rupees for an hour's work."

The next week, her price card said ninety rupees. She lost two buyers. But she stopped working till midnight, and her mother said she seemed less stressed.

I can't know everything she was thinking. But she looked like she'd found something out.

qa.q: How much did Gargi first charge per pair?
What might Gargi have been feeling as she stared at the page?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and a bit frustrated, realising how little she earned for an hour of work.

qa.q: What else could Gargi check about her new price?
qa.a: She could ask a few regular buyers whether ninety feels fair, or talk it through with a parent, before deciding whether to adjust again.

qa.q: How did the change look to Hemant?
qa.a: To Hemant it looked like she stopped working till midnight and seemed less stressed, though Hemant can't know all her thoughts.

grounding: An observer describes a student adding material costs and hours, comparing local prices and setting a fairer price, realising underpricing made the work unsustainable.

subtype: Approach: pricing by costs and time [Thinking]
passage:
Week 1: Pradeep started repairing bicycles for neighbours in the colony, charging fifty rupees a job because his friend Yogesh said, "Keep it cheap, people will love you." He was busy every evening.

Week 3: Pradeep sat with a notebook, thinking aloud. "Puncture patch, cement and a new valve: thirty rupees. Time: forty minutes. Walking to the shop for parts: another twenty." He looked at Yogesh. "I'm working for almost nothing. And I'm too tired to study." Yogesh shrugged. "But everyone's happy."

Week 5: Pradeep had checked the shop near the market: they charged a hundred and twenty for the same repair. He made a small card: eighty rupees, parts included. He showed it to his father first, who said it seemed fair. Two neighbours grumbled. Most didn't. He now had fewer jobs, but he finished by seven and had time for homework.

qa.q: What did the shop near the market charge for the same repair?
How did Pradeep feel in week 3 as he worked out his numbers?
qa.a: Pradeep felt tired and frustrated, realising he was working for almost nothing.

qa.q: What else could Pradeep consider as the business grows?
qa.a: He could keep a record of costs each month and talk with his father before any further change, so the price stays fair to both sides.

qa.q: How might the neighbours who grumbled see the new price?
qa.a: They may feel a little annoyed at first, but still see it as cheaper than the shop and convenient.

grounding: Shows a student adding material costs and time, comparing a local shop's price and setting a fairer price after realising underpricing was unsustainable.
